In simple terms: When you place a ‘buy AAPL at $150’ order, the system needs to find a matching ‘sell AAPL at $150’ order. This must happen in microseconds, correctly, and never match the same order twice.

Designing a Stock Broker Platform (Robinhood / Zerodha)

Simulate this design Draw it from memory

Difficulty: Advanced Topics: Order Matching, Event Sourcing, CQRS, Kafka, Delivery Semantics Asked at: Robinhood, Zerodha, Groww, Upstox, Goldman Sachs Prerequisites:Event Sourcing, Message Queues, and Idempotency

1. Understanding the Problem

A stock broker platform lets retail users buy and sell financial instruments (stocks, ETFs, options). The broker receives user orders, validates them against account balances and risk rules, routes them to an exchange (or internal matching engine), and shows real-time status updates. The system must handle thousands of concurrent orders during market hours with strong consistency guarantees - a lost or duplicate trade is a regulatory violation.

2. Naive First Cut

New components:

  • API Server: One process taking the order, checking the balance, and calling the exchange, all inside the user’s request.
  • Postgres DB: Orders, balances and positions in one database, holding only each order’s current state.
  • Exchange (NSE or BSE): The National and Bombay Stock Exchanges - the outside venues where an order actually meets a counterparty. Calling them synchronously is what makes this sketch fragile, because their latency becomes our latency.

How this breaks:

  • Single API server can’t handle 50K orders/sec during market open
  • Synchronous exchange call blocks the API - timeouts pile up
  • No order queue - if exchange is slow, user retries create duplicates
  • No way to notify users of fills without polling
  • Single DB becomes write bottleneck during peak hours
  • No audit trail - regulators require full event history of every order state change

The rest of the doc evolves this into a production-grade event-driven architecture.

3. Prior Art We’re Drawing From

  • Zerodha Kite OMS - Silo-based user partitioning, pre-trade validation at the gateway, async order routing to exchange. Handles millions of orders daily on commodity hardware. (zerodha.tech blog)💡 A silo is an independent group of users served by its own full copy of the stack, so a fault or a surge in one group cannot reach the others. OMS stands for order management system, the service that owns an order’s lifecycle.
  • LMAX Exchange Disruptor - Single-threaded matching engine processing 6M orders/sec using a lock-free ring buffer. Demonstrates that matching is CPU-bound, not I/O-bound.💡 LMAX’s finding is counter-intuitive and this design leans on it throughout: one thread handling a symbol’s orders in order beats many threads coordinating, because the coordination costs more than the matching. A ring buffer is the fixed-size circular array it hands work through without taking locks.
  • Coinbase Matching Engine - Continuous first-come-first-serve order book with price-time priority. Publishes trade events via WebSocket feed. (Coinbase docs)
  • Kafka + Flink for Exchange - Event-driven architecture where every state change is a Kafka event; Flink processes matching and settlement in real-time streams. (Medium article)💡 Flink is a stream-processing engine: it reads an endless feed of events and keeps running state in memory, checkpointing it so a crash resumes rather than restarts.
  • Robinhood - Routes orders to market makers (payment-for-order-flow, or PFOF, model) rather than running own matching engine.💡 Under payment for order flow the broker hands customer orders to a trading firm that pays for them, instead of matching the orders itself. It is worth knowing because it changes which half of this design you actually need to build. Emphasizes idempotent order submission and real-time push notifications.

4. Functional Requirements

Core (Top 3)

  1. Place and match buy/sell orders - submit limit/market orders, match based on price-time priority💡 A market order says “buy now at whatever the going price is”; a limit order says “buy only at this price or better, and wait otherwise”. Price-time priority means the best price is filled first, and among orders at the same price the one that arrived first is filled first. These two rules are the whole of Deep Dive 1.
  2. Show users their transactions - real-time order status, trade history, portfolio positions
  3. Send notifications - push notifications on order fills, partial fills, rejections, price alerts

Below the Line

  • Watchlists and price charts (read-heavy, CDN-cacheable)
  • Margin trading and short selling
  • Options and derivatives
  • Admin dashboard and compliance reporting
  • Referral and rewards system

5. Non-Functional Requirements

Core

Non-functional requirement (NFR) Target
Latency Order placement < 50ms P99 - the latency 99% of requests beat (broker side); matching < 5ms
Throughput 50K orders/sec at market open
Consistency Exactly-once order execution - no duplicates, no lost fills
Availability 99.99% during market hours (09:15 - 15:30 IST)
scroll →

💡 Exactly-once means every order is executed one time, never zero and never twice. It is the hardest guarantee in distributed systems because the network can always lose the acknowledgement rather than the work, and Deep Dives 2 and 6 are both about earning it.

Below the Line

  • Audit trail retained for 7 years (regulatory)
  • Multi-region disaster recovery (DR) (but matching engine is single-leader)💡 Single-leader means exactly one machine is allowed to decide the order of events for a symbol at any time. It is what makes price-time priority meaningful, and it is also why the matching tier cannot simply be run in two regions at once.
  • Sub-second portfolio updates after fills

6. Scale Estimation (Back-of-Envelope)

  • Users: 5M daily active users (DAU), 500K+ concurrent at market open (09:15 IST)💡 Back-of-envelope estimation is the rough arithmetic you do before choosing any component, so each pick is defended by a number. Learn more →
  • Write QPS (queries per second): 10M orders/day over a 6.25-hour session averages only ~450/sec, but the load is brutally front-loaded. Roughly 80% arrives in the first 30 minutes (~4.5K/sec across that window), and the opening seconds peak near 50K orders/sec – about 100x the daily average. That peak is the number to design against; the average is irrelevant.
  • Read QPS: 100K price updates/sec streaming to clients (5000 symbols × 20 updates/sec each)
  • Storage: ~2TB trade history/year (10M trades/day × trade + fill + audit event metadata)
  • Bandwidth: ~3 gigabits per second (Gbps) at peak (WebSocket price streams + order confirmations to 500K clients)

7. Core Entities

  • User - account, KYC status, cash balance, margin
  • Order - symbol, side (buy/sell), type (market/limit), quantity, price, status, timestamps
  • Trade (Fill) - matched order pair, execution price, quantity, timestamp
  • Position - user’s holding in a symbol (quantity, avg price)
  • Notification - type, user, payload, delivery status
  • OrderBook - per-symbol sorted structure of active limit orders

8. API / System Interface

POST /api/v1/orders
  Body: { symbol, side: "BUY"|"SELL", type: "MARKET"|"LIMIT", quantity, price?, idempotencyKey }

  Response: { orderId, status: "ACCEPTED", timestamp }
  Auth: JWT Bearer token
  Note: idempotencyKey prevents duplicate submissions on retry


GET /api/v1/orders?status=FILLED&from=2026-01-01&to=2026-06-25&page=1
  Response: { orders: [...], pagination: { total, page, pageSize } }

GET /api/v1/portfolio
  Response: { cash, positions: [{ symbol, quantity, avgPrice, currentPrice, pnl }] }

GET /api/v1/orders/{orderId}
  Response: { order details + fills }

WebSocket /ws/v1/orders
  Pushes: { type: "ORDER_UPDATE", orderId, status, filledQty, ... }

9. High-Level Design

FR1: Place and Match Orders

The first thing a user does is place a buy or sell order. Let’s build the simplest path for that.

New components we need:

  1. API Gateway - Entry point for all requests. Handles auth (JSON Web Token, or JWT) and rate limiting.
  2. Order Management Service (OMS) - The brain. Validates orders (enough balance? valid symbol? market open?), persists them, and publishes events.
  3. Kafka - Our event bus.💡 Kafka is a distributed log where events are appended and consumed by multiple services independently. Think of it as a super-reliable conveyor belt for messages. Learn more →
  4. Matching Engine - Consumes order events and pairs buyers with sellers.
  5. Order DB (Postgres) - Stores all orders and their current state. Source of truth.

Step-by-step flow:

  1. User taps “Buy 10 RELIANCE at ₹2,850” in the app → request hits API Gateway
  2. Gateway checks: Is the user authenticated? Is the user within rate limits?
  3. Gateway forwards to OMS. OMS validates: Does the user have enough cash? Is RELIANCE a valid symbol? Is the market open?
  4. OMS persists the order in Postgres with status PENDING and blocks ₹28,500 from the user’s available balance (soft hold - money isn’t gone yet, just reserved)
  5. OMS publishes an order.placed event to Kafka, partitioned by symbol
  6. User gets back 202 Accepted with their orderId - they don’t wait for matching

Why Kafka between OMS and Matching Engine?

The matching engine processes orders one at a time per symbol. If OMS waited for matching synchronously, every order would block. Instead: OMS responds instantly (“accepted”), matching happens async. The user gets notified when their order fills.

Why partition by symbol?

All orders for RELIANCE must be matched in strict price-time order. Kafka guarantees ordering within a partition. So we put all RELIANCE orders in one partition → one consumer processes them sequentially → no distributed locks needed.💡 This is the trick worth remembering: if only one worker ever touches a thing, there is nothing to coordinate. Partitioning for ordering buys away the entire locking problem - and Deep Dive 4 is the bill for it.

What FR1 leaves broken: three things, and the first is the one that ends careers.

  • A retry places a second order. The Idempotency-Key header is in the API contract and nothing reads it. The user’s phone drops its connection after the OMS commits but before the 202 arrives, the app retries exactly as it should, and the user buys twenty shares. At 50K orders/sec through Indian mobile networks at market open this is not a rare case, and a double fill is a reportable incident rather than a bug. Deep Dive 6.
  • Matching is hand-waved. “Pairs buyers with sellers” is doing a lot of work. The obvious implementation is to scan the open orders for this symbol looking for a counterparty, which is linear in book depth on every single order.💡 “Book depth” is how many open orders are sitting on a symbol waiting for a counterparty. Linear means the work per incoming order grows in step with that number, so the busiest symbol at the busiest moment is also the slowest. Deep Dive 1 builds the real structure.
  • One partition per symbol is one consumer per symbol. That is exactly what gives us ordering, and it means RELIANCE’s matching throughput is capped at whatever one thread can do. On a normal afternoon that is plenty. At 09:15, when the hot symbols take 10x the order flow of everything else, it is the bottleneck. Deep Dive 4.

FR2: Show Users Their Transactions

Once orders are filled, users need to see their transaction history and portfolio. The data is already in Postgres, so the simplest thing that works is to read it back out.

New components:

  1. Query Service - Serves all read requests: portfolio, order history, open orders.

A portfolio is not a stored thing here. It is derived: sum the fills per symbol, weight by execution price, and you have the position. So the Query Service computes it per request.

Step-by-step flow:

  1. User opens the “My Orders” or portfolio screen
  2. Gateway routes to the Query Service
  3. Query Service runs the read against the same Postgres the OMS writes to – a join across orders, fills and the user’s cash row
  4. Positions are aggregated per symbol on the fly, so the number on screen is always exactly consistent with the orders that produced it

What FR2 leaves broken: the reads are correct and they are pointed at the wrong database.

In simple terms: User opens the app to check their holdings. This read is 100x more frequent than trades. If we query the same database that handles trading, read traffic slows down trades.

  • Portfolio reads land on the write primary. Users refresh constantly, especially when the market is moving, so reads outnumber trades by roughly 100 to 1. At market open that primary is already absorbing 50K order writes/sec and we are now also asking it to run multi-table aggregations. The read query is not the problem; the contention is. Deep Dive 5 separates the paths.
  • Recomputing the portfolio per request is wasteful in a specific way. The aggregate only changes when a fill happens, which for most users is a handful of times a day, and we recompute it on every screen open.
  • And there is a regulatory requirement this cannot meet at all. SEBI and the SEC expect an answer to “what was the state of order X at 10:32:47.123?”.💡 The Securities and Exchange Board of India and the US Securities and Exchange Commission - the two market regulators. Their demand for point-in-time history is a functional requirement in disguise, and it is what forces the event log in Deep Dive 5. An orders table holds current state and overwrites history, so that question has no answer here. Deep Dive 5 turns out to solve both problems with one mechanism.

FR3: Send Notifications

When a user’s order fills, we need to tell them. The event is already on Kafka, so something consumes it and sends a push notification to their phone.

New components:

  1. Notification Service - Consumes fill/reject events from Kafka, resolves user preferences, and routes to the right channel.
  2. FCM / APNs - Firebase Cloud Messaging (Android) and Apple Push Notification Service (iOS). External services that deliver push notifications to locked phones.
  3. Dead Letter Queue (DLQ) - Where failed notifications go for retry.💡 A DLQ is a holding pen for messages that couldn’t be processed. A separate job retries them later instead of losing them.

Step-by-step flow:

  1. trade.executed event arrives at Notification Service from Kafka
  2. Service looks up user preferences: do they want push? email? SMS? in-app only?
  3. Templates the message: “Your order to BUY 10 RELIANCE filled at ₹2,847 ✓”
  4. Sends via FCM/APNs, retrying with exponential backoff (1s, 2s, 4s, 8s…) on failure💡 Exponential backoff doubles the wait between attempts. It matters because a failing dependency is usually overloaded, and retrying at full speed is how a brief wobble becomes an outage.
  5. Permanently failed deliveries → DLQ. A reconciler job retries every 5 minutes or flags for manual review.
  6. Meanwhile a user who is actively watching the app polls GET /orders/{id} every second to see the status change

Delivery semantics:

  • Notifications: at-least-once - getting “Order filled” twice is annoying but harmless💡 At-least-once means a message may be delivered more than once but never dropped. It is the cheap default, and this line is the design deciding where that default is acceptable and where it is not.
  • Order execution: exactly-once - filling an order twice is a regulatory violation, and nothing in the design so far delivers it

What FR3 leaves broken: a user staring at the screen while their order fills is the single most latency-sensitive moment in the product, and polling is the one thing we have given them. A one-second poll from 500K concurrent users at market open is 500K requests/sec of “has anything happened yet”, against a design whose entire order write path is 50K/sec. The read tier costs ten times the write tier, to deliver an answer that is on average half a second stale. Deep Dive 3 earns the push channel – and the interesting part there is not the WebSocket, it is how a fill event finds the one server holding that user’s connection.

10. Technology Choices

Tier Purpose Stores Access Pattern Primary Alternatives
Order Book (hot) Active limit orders Open orders per symbol Price-time sorted insert/remove In-memory TreeMap per symbol Redis Sorted Set, LMAX Disruptor
Order DB Order state and history All orders ever placed Write-heavy during market, read for history Postgres (partitioned by date) CockroachDB, TiDB
Event Bus Order events stream Events: placed, matched, filled, rejected Append-only, partitioned by symbol Kafka Redpanda, Kinesis
Portfolio Store User holdings and balances Positions, cash, P&L Read-heavy, write on fills Postgres (CQRS read replica) DynamoDB, ScyllaDB
Notification Queue Push delivery Notification payloads Fan-out per user Kafka + FCM/APNs SQS + SNS
Cache Market data, session Prices, user sessions High-QPS reads Redis Cluster Memcached
Object Store Trade confirmations, reports PDFs, CSVs Batch reads S3 GCS, MinIO
scroll →

💡 A TreeMap keeps its keys sorted, so the best bid or the best ask is always the first entry and inserting a new price level stays cheap. That single property is why the order book lives in memory rather than in a database.

Why Postgres for the order DB, not DynamoDB? Orders are relational (order → fills → settlements), need ACID transactions (atomicity, consistency, isolation, durability) for balance deductions, and regulators require complex queries for audits. Postgres with partitioning by date handles the write volume. The matching engine itself uses in-memory structures - the DB is for persistence, not matching speed.

Why Kafka, not a simple queue? Orders need event replay (for reconciliation), partitioning by symbol (for ordered matching), and multiple consumers (matcher, notifier, portfolio updater, audit logger). Kafka’s log-based model fits perfectly.

11. Data Modeling

In-Memory TreeMap (Order Book — active limit orders per symbol):

Structure per symbol:
  BuyOrders:  TreeMap<Price DESC, Queue<Order>>   -- highest buy price first
  SellOrders: TreeMap<Price ASC, Queue<Order>>    -- lowest sell price first
  
Each Order: { orderId, userId, side, price, remainingQty, timestamp }
Match condition: topBuy.price >= topSell.price → execute trade

Postgres (Order DB — all orders ever placed, partitioned by date):

CREATE TABLE orders (
    order_id UUID NOT NULL,
    user_id UUID NOT NULL,
    symbol VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    side VARCHAR(4) NOT NULL,       -- BUY, SELL
    order_type VARCHAR(6) NOT NULL, -- MARKET, LIMIT
    quantity INTEGER NOT NULL,
    price DECIMAL(12,4),
    filled_quantity INTEGER DEFAULT 0,
    status VARCHAR(10) NOT NULL,    -- ACCEPTED, PARTIAL, FILLED, CANCELLED, REJECTED
    idempotency_key UUID,
    created_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
    updated_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL,
    -- Postgres requires every unique/primary key on a partitioned table to
    -- include the partition key, so created_at joins both constraints.
    PRIMARY KEY (order_id, created_at),
    UNIQUE (idempotency_key, created_at)
) PARTITION BY RANGE (created_at);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_user ON orders(user_id, created_at DESC);
CREATE INDEX idx_orders_symbol ON orders(symbol, status);

CREATE TABLE trades (
    trade_id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    buy_order_id UUID NOT NULL,
    sell_order_id UUID NOT NULL,
    symbol VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    price DECIMAL(12,4) NOT NULL,
    quantity INTEGER NOT NULL,
    executed_at TIMESTAMP NOT NULL
);
SQL

Postgres (Portfolio Store — user holdings):

CREATE TABLE positions (
    user_id UUID NOT NULL,
    symbol VARCHAR(20) NOT NULL,
    quantity INTEGER NOT NULL,
    avg_buy_price DECIMAL(12,4) NOT NULL,
    PRIMARY KEY (user_id, symbol)
);

CREATE TABLE balances (
    user_id UUID PRIMARY KEY,
    available_cash DECIMAL(14,2) NOT NULL,
    reserved_cash DECIMAL(14,2) NOT NULL DEFAULT 0  -- locked for open orders
);
SQL

Kafka (Event Bus — order events partitioned by symbol):

Topic: order-events (partitioned by symbol)
  Key: symbol
  Value: { event_type, order_id, user_id, symbol, price, quantity, timestamp }
  Events: PLACED, MATCHED, PARTIALLY_FILLED, FILLED, CANCELLED, REJECTED

Access Patterns:

Query Data Source How
Place order In-memory matching engine Add to TreeMap, attempt immediate match, write result to Postgres + Kafka
Match orders In-memory Compare top of buy and sell trees; execute if prices cross
Get portfolio Postgres (read replica) SELECT * FROM positions WHERE user_id = ?
Order history Postgres SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC
Live price updates WebSocket + Redis Pub/Sub Matching engine publishes to price:{symbol} channel on every trade
scroll →

How the Matching Engine Executes a Trade:

  1. New BUY LIMIT order arrives: price=$150, qty=100 for AAPL
  2. Check sell side: topSell.price = $149.50 → $149.50 ≤ $150, so match is possible
  3. Execute at $149.50 (price-time priority): fill min(buyQty, sellQty) = min(100, 50) = 50 shares
  4. Create trade record, update both orders (buy: filled_qty += 50, sell: fully filled → remove from book)
  5. Buy order has 50 remaining → stays in the order book at $150, wait for next seller
  6. Publish PARTIALLY_FILLED event to Kafka → portfolio service updates positions, notification service alerts user
  7. All of this happens in-memory in ~10μs. Persistence to Postgres is async (write-behind via Kafka consumer)💡 Write-behind means the authoritative change happens in memory first and the database copy is written shortly after, rather than the match waiting on a disk. The in-memory book is the truth during the trading session; Postgres is the record of it.

12. Deep Dives

Deep Dive 1: Two orders cross at the same price and the same instant. Who gets filled first?

Bad: what FR1 left unspecified – scan the symbol’s open orders looking for a counterparty.

  • O(n) in book depth on every incoming order. A liquid symbol like RELIANCE carries tens of thousands of resting limit orders, so each of the 50K orders/sec arriving at market open walks a list of that size.💡 A resting order is one sitting in the book waiting for a counterparty - it has not been filled and has not been cancelled. The resting orders are the book. The work grows as the product of order rate and book depth, and both peak at the same moment.
  • It is also silently unfair, which matters more than the latency. Scanning in whatever order rows come back means two orders resting at the same price fill in arbitrary order. Price-time priority is not a performance optimisation here – an exchange that fills the later order first is one regulators take an interest in.

what FR1 left unspecified – scan the symbol’s open orders looking for a counterparty.

Sorted data structure (TreeMap/BST) keyed by price. Buy side = max-heap (highest bid first). Sell side = min-heap (lowest ask first). O(log n) insert, O(1) match against best price.

In-memory order book per symbol using two TreeMaps (bids descending, asks ascending). Each price level holds a FIFO queue of orders at that price. Match = peek best opposing side, if prices cross, execute.

When a BUY order arrives at price P:

Single-threaded per symbol - no locks needed. Borrowing from LMAX Disruptor: one thread per symbol partition achieves millions of matches/sec.

Deep Dive 2: A fill is worth money. How do we guarantee it happens once and not twice?

Bad: FR1’s chain, where every hop is at-least-once and nothing dedupes.

  • The OMS publishes to Kafka and does not wait for the ack, so a broker failover loses the order: the user holds a 202 Accepted for an order that will never match. Or the publish succeeds and the ack is lost, the OMS retries, and the same order is matched twice.
  • Downstream is no better. The Matching Engine processes a batch, writes the fills, and dies before committing its offset. Kafka redelivers, the engine matches the same orders again, and the user is filled twice at possibly a different price.
  • One double fill is a reportable incident, not a metric. This is the deep dive where “at-least-once is fine, callers should be idempotent” stops being an acceptable answer, because the caller here is a stranger’s money.

FR1’s chain, where every hop is at-least-once and nothing dedupes.

Idempotency key on order submission + DB unique constraint. Kafka consumer with manual offset commit after processing.

End-to-end exactly-once via the following chain:

compares Kafka events vs DB state every 5 minutes. Flags discrepancies for manual review. In 4 years at Zerodha, reconciler catches < 0.001% of trades.

Deep Dive 3: A fill event lands. Which of our 200 servers is holding that user’s connection?

Bad: the one-second poll from FR3.

  • 500K concurrent users at market open polling once a second is 500K requests/sec, ten times the order write rate, to deliver an answer that is half a second stale on average.
  • The cost is not just the volume, it is that it scales with idle users rather than with events. A user watching a position that does not move all morning generates 3,600 requests an hour and receives no information.

the one-second poll from FR3.

WebSocket connection per user, server pushes events.

Pub/Sub fan-out with connection registry:

Kafka guarantees durability but adds latency. WebSocket delivery is best-effort and ephemeral - if the push fails, the notification still gets sent via FCM as backup. Redis Pub/Sub is sub-millisecond.

Deep Dive 4: Ordering needs one consumer per symbol and RELIANCE needs four. Which do you give up?

Problem: Market opens at 09:15 IST. 80% of the day’s orders arrive in the first 30 minutes, with the opening seconds near 50K/sec. And the load is not spread evenly across symbols – RELIANCE and the NIFTY futures take roughly 10x an average symbol’s flow.

Bad: FR1’s partitioning – one Kafka partition per symbol, which is also what gives us ordering.

  • One partition means one consumer, which means one thread matching that symbol. That is the design working as intended for 5,000 quiet symbols and failing for the handful that matter. RELIANCE and the NIFTY futures take roughly 10x the order flow of an average symbol, so their single consumer saturates while most of the fleet idles.
  • Note the trap: the obvious fix is more partitions per symbol, and that is exactly what the ordering guarantee forbids. Kafka orders within a partition and not across them, so splitting RELIANCE across four partitions means four independent matching threads with no agreement on time priority – which is the Deep Dive 1 fairness problem reintroduced through the back door.

FR1’s partitioning – one Kafka partition per symbol, which is also what gives us ordering.

Pre-split hot symbols into sub-partitions (e.g., RELIANCE-0 through RELIANCE-3). Round-robin incoming orders across sub-partitions. Each sub-partition has its own matching engine instance.

Adaptive partitioning (borrowing from Zerodha’s silo approach):

Queue depth . If any partition’s lag exceeds 1000 messages, auto-scale by spinning up additional consumer for that partition.

Deep Dive 5: Why does fixing the read load also answer what an order looked like at 10:32:47?

Bad: FR2’s design – read the write primary, and keep current state in an orders table.

  • The contention is the visible half. Portfolio aggregations run against the same Postgres taking 50K order writes/sec at market open, so the cheapest requests in the product compete with the only ones that cannot be slow.
  • The unfixable half is the table shape. UPDATE orders SET status='FILLED' destroys the previous state. A row tells you what an order is, never what it was, so “what was the state of order X at 10:32:47.123?” has no answer – not a slow answer, no answer. You cannot index your way out of data you overwrote.

FR2’s design – read the write primary, and keep current state in an table.

a read replica plus a Redis cache for portfolios.

make the event log the source of truth and treat current state as a projection.

on reads (200-500ms lag). Acceptable for portfolio views. Not acceptable for balance checks (those hit the write DB directly).

Deep Dive 6: The app retries a buy it already sent. What stops the user owning twice as much?

In simple terms: Your app’s network drops mid-trade. It retries. Without protection, you buy the same stock twice. We need to guarantee that retrying a request never causes double-execution.

Bad: FR1’s gateway, which accepts an Idempotency-Key header and ignores it.

  • The failure needs no exotic conditions. The OMS commits the order, the 202 is lost on a patchy mobile connection, the app retries because that is the correct thing for a client to do, and the user now owns twenty shares of a stock they bought ten of.
  • It is invisible in testing, because nobody double-taps their own buy button on a fast local network against a stubbed broker. It shows up at market open on real networks, in money.

FR1’s gateway, which accepts an header and ignores it.

a unique constraint on the key.

store the response and replay it, so the retry is indistinguishable from the first call.

one extra write per order, in the same transaction. At 50K orders/sec that table is write-hot; partition by key hash, or do the check in Redis with a TTL and keep the unique constraint as the durable backstop.

13. Design Self-Audit

Question Answer
Dedicated search index? Not needed - users search by symbol (indexed column), not free text
Stale reads after writes? Read-your-writes for order status via write-DB; portfolio via cache invalidation on fill
Single points of failure (SPOFs)? Matching engine is single-leader per symbol - failover via standby replica with Kafka replay
Dead-letter / reconciliation? ✅ Reconciler scans PENDING orders, DLQ for failed notifications
Data freshness across caches? Portfolio cache TTL 30s + event-driven invalidation on fills
Cost at scale? Kafka retention (7 years) → tier to S3 after 30 days. Matching engine is CPU-only, no expensive DB
scroll →

14. Core Flows

Flow 1: Order Placement End-to-End

Non-obvious failure path: If Kafka is temporarily unavailable after OMS persists the order, the order sits in PENDING state. A reconciler cron (every 30s) scans for orders stuck in PENDING > 60s and re-publishes them to Kafka. The matching engine is idempotent (uses orderId as dedup key), so re-publishing is safe.

Flow 2: Transaction History Query

Order State Machine

15. Final Architecture

New components: three boxes appear here that the functional requirements never introduced.

  • WebSocket Gateway: the push tier from Deep Dive 3. It holds one open connection per logged-in client and writes fills and price ticks down it, which is what replaces FR3’s one-second poll.
  • Cold Storage (old trades): object storage holding events older than the hot window. It exists because the seven-year audit requirement is cheap to satisfy on files and expensive to satisfy on a database.
  • Redis (hot quotes and balances): the in-memory tier the OMS checks for buying power before accepting an order, so a validation does not cost a database round trip on the 50K-orders-per-second path.

Drop a comment below if you want a specific deep dive expanded (margin trading, options settlement, Financial Information eXchange (FIX) protocol) 👇💡 FIX is the standard message format brokers and exchanges use to exchange orders and fills. If you connect to a real exchange, this is the wire protocol you speak.

How it works end-to-end:

  1. User places order — Mobile/Web hits Load Balancer → API Gateway → Order Management Service
  2. OMS validates and persists — checks idempotency, writes order to Postgres, emits event to Kafka
  3. Matching Engine consumes — picks up order from the per-symbol Kafka partition, matches against the in-memory order book (price-time priority)
  4. Fill event emitted — matched trade published back to Kafka
  5. Event Projector updates read stores — consumes fill events, updates Postgres Read Replica and Redis Cluster for portfolio/position queries
  6. Notification Service alerts user — push notification via FCM/APNs and real-time update via WebSocket Gateway
  7. Exchange integration — Matching Engine forwards orders to NSE/BSE for external execution
  8. Reconciler ensures consistency — compares internal state with exchange confirmations, fixes discrepancies
  9. Cold storage archival — Kafka sinks historical events to S3 for regulatory audit trail

Key Technologies

Term What it is
CQRS Command Query Responsibility Segregation - separating the fast write path (order placement) from the scalable read path (portfolio, history) so each scales independently.
Event Sourcing Storing every order state change as an immutable event in Kafka, enabling full audit replay and point-in-time reconstruction for regulators.
Kafka Distributed event log partitioned by symbol ensuring ordered matching per stock and enabling multiple independent consumers (matcher, notifier, auditor).
Order Matching Engine In-memory TreeMap-based order book with price-time priority - single-threaded per symbol for lock-free matching at millions of ops/sec.
WebSocket Persistent connection pushing real-time order fills and market price updates to active clients without polling.
Redis In-memory cache for market data, user sessions, portfolio snapshots, and Pub/Sub routing for WebSocket fan-out.
Postgres ACID relational DB for order state, balance management, and idempotency key storage with partitioning by date.
scroll →
Dead Letter Queue Holding queue for failed notifications or unprocessable events - retried by a sweeper or escalated for manual review.

What’s Expected at Each Level

This section helps you calibrate your depth. You don’t need to cover everything - just know what’s expected for your level.

Mid-level

Design a basic order placement and execution flow. Understand the need for an order book - that buy and sell orders must be matched by price. Propose a database for storing trades and a queue for processing orders asynchronously. With prompting, discuss why exactly-once delivery matters and what happens if an order is processed twice.

Senior

Propose event sourcing for the order lifecycle - every state change is an immutable event. Explain CQRS and why separating the write model from the read model matters for a broker. Discuss Kafka for event streaming with partitions ordered by symbol. Articulate idempotency for order submission (client-generated keys + DB unique constraints) and the need for sequence numbers to detect gaps.

Staff+

Address matching engine internals - price-time priority with a TreeMap per side, single-threaded per symbol partition (LMAX-style). Discuss market data fan-out to millions of clients via tiered pub-sub or multicast. Proactively mention regulatory requirements (7-year audit trail, trade reconstruction from event log), split-brain scenarios during network partition (matching engine is single-leader with standby failover),💡 Multicast puts one copy of a price update on the network and every subscribed machine receives it, instead of the server sending a separate copy per client. Split-brain is when a network fault leaves two halves of a cluster each believing it is the leader, so both accept orders and the two histories diverge - fatal when the leader’s job is deciding who was first. and the cost of real-time position calculation at scale.

🎯 Key Takeaways

  • Exactly-once via idempotency keys + Kafka transactions - no double fills

  • CQRS separates write path (fast, consistent) from read path (scalable, eventually consistent)
  • Partition by symbol in Kafka ensures ordered matching per stock
  • Reconciler catches edge cases that the primary path misses

Understand the building blocks used in this design:

  • Event Sourcing & CQRS → — order and trade events form the immutable audit log the system replays from
  • Message Queues → — feeds orders into the matching engine and fans out fills to downstream services
  • Idempotency → — a retried order submission never executes the same trade twice
  • WebSockets vs SSE → — streams live price ticks and order-status updates to clients
